text:
The woman who captured the video of her traffic stop with an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who had his gun drawn spoke out for the first time Wednesday.

Carolina Molina, a U.S. citizen, says she was driving to different immigration lawyers' offices in Falls Church, Virginia, to drop off business cards, when she saw ICE making arrests.

"He got out with a gun, pointed it to my head asking why I was following them around. I told them I was not, I was leaving cards," Molina said during a press conference Wednesday. "I think my life was in danger at that point."

She shared her dashcam video, showing her driving by officers and yelling at them.

Video provided to 7News shows an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent with his gun drawn toward a woman in Falls Church, Va. (Carolina Molina)

Soon after, she said she tried driving out of the parking lot, when her video captured the moments multiple ICE vehicles carried out the traffic stop.

The cell phone video she took while in the driver's seat shows one officer approaching her with his gun drawn.

"Yeah, you record us. You almost ran us over," the officer can be heard yelling in this video.

Molina responded, "I didn't almost run you over."

The back-and-forth continue for a few seconds, before the officer at the center of this can be heard telling Molina he will arrest her.

Video provided to 7News shows an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent with his gun drawn toward a woman in Falls Church, Va. (Carolina Molina)

Molina was not arrested, and drove off soon after this now-viral traffic stop.

"I am loudmouthed and I do feel, as an American citizen, I have a right to my first amendment," Molina said Wednesday. "I just don't think it's fair that they can sit there and block somebody in, and point a gun to your head and then get away with it. I think they should be investigated."

A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson provided the following statement:

On August 10, 2026, while ICE was conducting targeted immigration enforcement in Falls Church, Virginia, an anti-ICE agitator began to drive her car in circles around our ICE officers and then attempted to harm officers by weaponizing her vehicle against them—all in an attempt to help illegal aliens get away.

The operation was targeting criminal illegal aliens, whose crimes included a hit and run and drug trafficking, and illegal aliens with final orders of removal. Fearing for their safety, ICE officers conducted a vehicle stop of the driver. Necessary background information of the driver was taken and she could face criminal prosecution as a result of her actions.

Our officers are experiencing a more than 1,300% increase in assaults against them, a 3,300% increase in vehicular attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats. When faced with dangerous circumstances, DHS law enforcement used their training to protect themselves, their fellow officers, and the public.

7News On Your Side asked if ICE had their own evidence showing Molina weaponized her car, and how long the officer who had his gun drawn had been with the agency.

Nobody has responded to these follow-up questions as of publication of this article.

Molina denied the claims she weaponized her car.

We asked her if she had any encounters with ICE officers before the moments on video she shared, and said she had rolled down her window and shouted at different agents in another business park down the street.

"There was a time when I had driven out and I had seen them arresting someone, and I was just like, 'You're messed up, that's messed up what you're doing,' but they got into a car and left," Molina said.

title: Trump Administration's Grant Tactics Continue Troubling Trends - The Debt Dispatch
description:
Growth of Federal Grants is the Root Cause Crucially, the grants themselves are the root of the problem.

While local governments have a responsibility to address problems such as violent crime, it does not follow that funding should be routed through Washington.

text:
The Trump Administration is pressuring local governments to sign cooperation agreements with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) by threatening access to grants for ambulance services, police gear, and rape prosecutions. This escalation will lead to fresh rounds of litigation and policy uncertainty. If successful, it would establish a concerning precedent that would allow the executive branch to use the expansive volume of federal grants to coerce other levels of government into following a President’s policy agenda.

Turning Grants into a Power Grab

With many state and local governments refusing to use local resources to support deportation efforts, the Trump Administration has used a variety of methods in seeking to eliminate sanctuary policies. This includes attempting to claw back previously disbursed Homeland Security funding and issuing agency-wide memos freezing certain grants based on immigration policy demands. Affected governments sued to retain access to the funds. Although some cases remain ongoing, other cases led to courts blocking the administration’s moves.

While there will certainly be litigation regarding the administration’s latest approach, jurisdictions such as Miami are choosing to cooperate rather than risk losing access to the grants for an unknown amount of time.

Since the latest move by the Trump Administration has not yet been blocked, it is important to recognize that it represents an attempted power grab on two different fronts.

First, Congress never authorized linking these grants to cooperation with ICE, meaning that the executive branch is attempting to usurp the legislative branch’s authority. Second, the executive branch is attempting to control policy at the state and local level. If courts do not rule against the administration, it would encourage similar tactics in the future, with potential ramifications across the spectrum of domestic policy areas.

Presidents of Both Parties Using Grant Coercion

This is not the first time that an administration has sought to use federal grants to dictate policy to state and local governments.

Starting in 2016, the Obama Administration (followed by the first Trump Administration) attempted to use Department of Justice grants to get cities to cooperate with immigration-related demands. This led to years of litigation, with most courts ultimately ruling against the federal government. Outside of the immigration space, the Obama and Biden administrations sought to use grants to dictate policies related to gender identity in schools, though both were eventually blocked in court.

The Trump Administration’s attempt to use federal grants to obtain cooperation with ICE is also an example of the degradation of the separation of powers, as governing power is increasingly concentrated in the White House.

Growth of Federal Grants is the Root Cause

Crucially, the grants themselves are the root of the problem. State and local governments receive federal funding for a variety of functions that are not proper federal concerns. In the current fight, these include local law enforcement, social programs, and disaster response. While local governments have a responsibility to address problems such as violent crime, it does not follow that funding should be routed through Washington. Perversely, it is the importance of such activities that makes the administration’s coercion more effective.

State and local governments have become increasingly dependent on more than $1 trillion per year in federal handouts for everything from police and first responders to education and health care, which gives Washington the ability to coerce state and local policies. Without this dependence, the Trump Administration would lose its (legally arguable) leverage over cooperation with ICE.

Further, state and local governance should not depend on an increasingly dysfunctional and heavily indebted federal government, and the staggering volume of grant programs means that Congress is unable to provide meaningful oversight of most of them.

Congress Can Stop Grant-Based Coercion

Congress should rein in the Trump Administration’s overreach. For example, the Senate added language to a Continuing Resolution pushing back against the administration’s proposed rulemaking that would centralize grantmaking power with political appointees. While the administration’s separate immigration-related grant maneuver would be more complicated to stop, Congress should still intervene.

More fundamentally, Congress should simply reduce the number and funding level of federal grant programs, with the goal of eliminating them altogether. Drawing down federal aid to state and local governments would reduce the deficit while also rebalancing the distribution of power in a manner that is healthier for American democracy. Most of the programs in question are funded through the appropriations process. Changing course will require moving away from the habit of governing with various forms of continuing resolutions and instead scrutinizing programs that are not related to proper federal responsibilities.

Congress should not only block the administration’s power grab but also reduce the incentive for similar power grabs by reducing the amount of power that flows through federal grants.

text:
FAIRFAX COUNTY, Va. (DC News Now) — The Fairfax County Commonwealth’s Attorney’s Office said it is reviewing an encounter captured on video in which an ICE agent pointed a gun at a Northern Virginia woman who had shouted at agents conducting arrests in a parking lot.

Carolina Molina, a licensed professional counselor, spoke Tuesday alongside local immigrant-rights groups in the same office park where the incident unfolded. She said she was dropping off business cards at immigration law offices in the Falls Church area when she saw agents making arrests Monday.

Molina said she yelled at an agent from her car, then tried to leave the parking lot. Dashcam and cellphone video show ICE vehicles pulling in front of and behind her car before an agent approached her driver’s-side window with a gun drawn.

“You almost ran us over,” the agent said in the video.

Molina denied following or threatening the agents.

“I think my life was in danger at that point,” she said at the news conference. “I think they should be investigated, and if their body cam was on, then put it out there.”

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said Molina drove in circles around ICE officers and tried to harm them by “weaponizing” her vehicle. DHS said officers were conducting a targeted operation involving people with criminal histories and final removal orders, and stopped Molina because they feared for their safety.

The agency said Molina could face criminal prosecution. She was not arrested or charged during the encounter.

The Commonwealth’s Attorney’s Office said it has heard from concerned community members, is aware of the incident and is reviewing it. The office did not provide further details.

text:
WASHINGTON —

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents could soon be given a new tool: gloves that are designed to deliver an electric shock.

As President Donald Trump's mass deportation campaign continues, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security is planning to spend up to $20 million to obtain devices known as G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, according to a notice first reported by the Associated Press.

DHS didn't directly respond to emailed questions on Wednesday about how soon the devices could be deployed and how widespread the uptake might be in the field, but the size of the purchase suggests that ICE is preparing to equip a large portion of its agents.

In a statement that does not explicitly mention the gloves, an unnamed DHS spokesperson wrote, "ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country."

"Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards," the statement added.

The manufacturer, Compliant Technologies, said the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until they're activated by an officer. They're designed to deliver a painful voltage when applied directly to a person's skin, a strategy that could be used to de-escalate when a person is resisting arrest or threatening an agent.

The device has been used by some jails and police departments in the past, but critics are concerned that ICE could abuse the gloves as a punishment tool, as some agents face allegations of excessive force.

During a press conference on Wednesday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and the state's attorney general, Letitia James, warned of potential legal action if the tool is misused.

"That appears to me on its face to be a violation of civil rights to cause that kind of physical harm to an individual, regardless of what the offense may be," Hochul said.

Asked what circumstances would warrant the use of these gloves, DHS didn't provide specifics. However, an agency spokesperson noted that officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use-of-force training.

The manufacturer warns that the gloves, which are marketed as nonlethal, should not be used in response to verbal defiance or for punishment. They should also not be used against the elderly, small children, pregnant women, and the severely handicapped.

The Trump administration is also in the process of deploying body cameras across the country. One month ago, DHS said that body cameras had been sent to more than half of ICE field offices and that the remainder would get them within 60 days.

The timeline came under scrutiny earlier this summer after two deaths involving ICE agents who weren't wearing body cameras at the time of those incidents.

Funding for the expansion was authorized by Congress earlier this year, emerging as one of the few areas of common ground as lawmakers sparred over ICE reform.
